vignette:
Anand had dedicated his life to quiet service. At sixty-eight, his work at a small non-profit providing resources to new immigrants was the central pillar of a life he had carefully rebuilt after his divorce years ago. That life ended six months ago in the concrete stairwell of his own apartment building. He was returning late from a fundraising dinner when a man emerged from the shadows beneath the landing. The assault was a blur of brutal force and chilling whispers, but certain sensory details had burned themselves into his memory: the scraping sound of the attacker's shoe on the gritty floor, the low, guttural commands spoken close to his ear, and the sharp, radiating pain in his back and hips as he was slammed against the cold cinderblock wall.

In the weeks that followed, Anand told no one, cloaking himself in a shame that felt as heavy as a physical weight. The event refused to stay in the past. It would surge forward without warning, not as a coherent story, but in vicious fragments. While sorting mail at the office, he would suddenly hear that whispered voice in his head, so clearly it felt as if the man were standing right behind him. The memory would bring with it a phantom agony, a deep, searing ache in his lower back that was so intense he would have to grip his desk to stay upright. He knew precisely what had happened to him, but when he tried to form the words, even in the privacy of his own mind, his thoughts would scatter. The vocabulary to describe the violation felt impossibly distant, locked away in a part of his brain he could no longer access.

His sense of safety was shattered. The familiar sounds of his apartment building-the rumble of the elevator, the creak of a neighbor's floorboards-were no longer benign. Each noise was a potential threat, a sign that someone was entering his space, and he found himself spending hours by the door, listening. At work, a colleague once gently touched his shoulder to ask a question, and Anand reacted with a choked gasp, stumbling back and sending a stack of files scattering across the floor. The colleague's startled apology only amplified his own humiliation. He saw himself through their eyes: a frail, jumpy old man. This belief that he was fundamentally broken, a lousy coper who couldn't handle what had happened, began to take root.

His routines calcified into a set of rigid, protective rules. He would never sit in a chair unless his back was flush against a wall, his eyes fixed on the entrance to the room. The fear of being alone became all-consuming, especially at night. He began staying at the non-profit until well after dark, organizing files that were already organized, reading reports he had already read, just to delay the inevitable return to his empty apartment. The silence there seemed to amplify the intrusive sounds in his head. During one particularly bad evening, trapped in a loop of the attacker's voice and the memory of the pain, he felt an overwhelming pressure build inside him. Desperate for a different sensation, he dug the nails of one hand into his opposite forearm, pressing down until the skin broke. The sharp, clean pain was a momentary release, a distraction from the agony he couldn't control.

He felt irrevocably cut off from the world around him. He would watch his younger colleagues laugh in the breakroom and feel a profound sense of alienation, as if he were watching a film of a life he could no longer participate in. He was an outsider now, permanently changed. The simple pleasure he once took in his work, the quiet satisfaction of helping a family navigate a new country, had been replaced by a persistent, dull numbness punctuated by spikes of terror. He became convinced that his ability to feel normal emotions was gone forever, a casualty of the violence he had endured. He finally sought an appointment after his program director, with gentle concern, asked about the long hours and the fresh, deep scratches on his arm. The inquiry, though kind, felt like a spotlight, exposing the private ruin he had tried so hard to conceal. He arrived at the clinic not with any real hope, but with the quiet terror that he was disappearing, and the even greater fear that it was already too late.
